Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

friend noun

also friends, playmate, pal, best friend, she’s my best friend, my best friend, chum, buddy

classical

Cic. Amic. 64: amīcus certus in rē incertā cernitur (Ennius)
Traupman 40: cum amīcīs meīs lūdō

amīcus, amīcī m.

noun, second declension

The plain word, for a friend of any age; the vocative amīce is the “friend!” of the fables.

Other words

  • amīca, amīcae f. — a girl’s or woman’s friend

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Ter. Hec. 4.2.16 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 37: Amīcae meae mē exspectant

    Lewis & Short calls this sense “very rare”: in comedy an amīca is usually a man’s mistress. Harmless for a small girl’s friends; sodālis or aequālis avoids the overtone.

  • sodālis, sodālis m./f. — mate, companion

    noun, third declension, masculine or feminine · also used · classical · Plaut. Merc. 2.4.7: tuos amīcus et sodālis (Lewis & Short); Traupman 291

    A favourite word of Plautus; Lewis & Short gives it common gender.

  • aequālis, aequālis m./f. — a child of the same age; playmate

    noun, third declension, masculine or feminine · also used · classical · Cic. Fin. 5.42; Plin. Ep. 9.33.4: redditque terrae et aequālibus

    The friends a small child plays with are his age-mates.

  • collūsor, collūsōris m. — playmate

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Plin. Ep. 9.33.8: gestātōrem collūsōremque puerōrum; Cic. Phil. 2.56 (Lewis & Short)

    Pliny’s word for the dolphin that played with the boys of Hippo; in Cicero, a partner at dice.

  • amīcus summus (amīca summa) — best friend

    summus, “highest”, with the noun · also used · classical · Ter. Ph. 5.8.60; 1.1.1; Ter. And. 5.6.6: amīcus summus, the best friend (Lewis & Short), s.v. superus; Traupman 98: amīca summa mea est

Examples

  • vetus verbum hoc quidem est: commūnia esse amīcōrum inter sē omnia

    it’s an old saying: friends share everythingTer. Ad. 803–804

  • dēscende, amīce

    come down, friend!Phaedr. 4.9.8

  • deinde aequālibus dēlectantur libenterque sē cum iīs congregant dantque sē ad lūdendum

    then they enjoy children of their own age, gladly join them and give themselves up to playCic. Fin. 5.42

See also enemy, share, play together.
